questions.q: What does it mean that Monte Carlo methods are 'model-free'?
options: They don't use a value function at all
They don't require knowledge of the transition probabilities P(s'|s,a) or reward function R(s,a,s')
They never use a discount factor
They can only be used with deterministic policies
questions.explain: Monte Carlo methods estimate value functions directly from sampled episodes, with no need to know the environment's transition or reward function in advance.

questions.q: How does Monte Carlo estimate V(s)?
options: By solving the Bellman equation analytically using known P and R
By averaging the actual observed returns G_t from every time state s was visited across episodes
By taking the maximum reward ever observed in state s
By always setting V(s) equal to the immediate reward
questions.explain: Monte Carlo approximates V^π(s) = E_π[G_t | S_t=s] empirically, averaging the real returns observed following visits to s, rather than computing the expectation analytically.

questions.q: What is the difference between first-visit and every-visit Monte Carlo?
options: First-visit only works for continuing tasks; every-visit only works for episodic tasks
First-visit uses only the return following the first visit to a state per episode; every-visit uses the return following every visit
First-visit requires a known model; every-visit does not
There is no practical difference between them
questions.explain: Both converge to the correct V^π(s), but first-visit MC counts only the first occurrence of a state per episode toward the average, while every-visit MC counts every occurrence.

questions.q: Why do Monte Carlo methods fundamentally require episodic tasks?
options: Because computing a return G_t requires summing reward all the way to the end of the episode
Because continuing tasks have no reward function
Because Monte Carlo cannot use a discount factor
Because episodic tasks have smaller state spaces
questions.explain: A Monte Carlo update needs the actual, complete return from a state onward, which means the episode must terminate before that return can be computed — this is incompatible with tasks that never end.

questions.q: In Monte Carlo control, what problem does 'exploring starts' solve?
options: It speeds up convergence of the discount factor
It guarantees every state-action pair is eventually visited, even under a greedy policy that might otherwise never try certain actions
It removes the need to compute returns
It converts an episodic task into a continuing one
questions.explain: Exploring starts force each episode to begin at a randomly chosen (state, action) pair, ensuring every action gets evaluated even if the policy being followed is otherwise greedy.
